performers: Orquesta Sinfónica de Madrid; Enrique Fernández Arbós
intro: In this Farruca from Falla’s ballet El sombrero de tres picos, the miller dances alone on St John’s Night. Enrique Fernández Arbós, who conducted the first performance of Falla’s Nights in 1916, conducted his Madrid orchestra in this Columbia recording of 1928.

C · Faster section to the final chords

cues.title: The Miller’s dance, St John’s Night
cues.text: On St John’s Night the neighbours gather at the mill, and the Miller’s Wife asks her husband to dance for them. He dances a farruca, which John Henken called “dark and fiery” and “the earthiest dance in the ballet”.
cues.evidence: The synopsis printed in the J. & W. Chester piano score (1921), Part II (1)–(3): the neighbours celebrate St John’s Night at the mill, the Miller’s Wife asks her husband to dance, “the miller’s dance”. John Henken, Los Angeles Philharmonic note on Suite No. 2: the miller’s solo is “a dark and fiery flamenco farruca, the earthiest dance in the ballet”. https://archive.org/details/elsombrerodetres00fall https://www.laphil.com/works/the-three-cornered-hat-suite-no-2

cues.title: Danse du Meunier, piano score
cues.text: The piano score marks the dance Moderato assai, “molto ritmico e pesante”. Heavy chords drop to a sudden pianissimo (“pp subito”) and grow louder again through a long “cresc. molto”, with a tune marked “il canto” above them.
cues.evidence: J. & W. Chester piano score (1921), Danse du Meunier, printed pages 38–40: Moderato assai (crotchet = 60), “ff molto ritmico e pesante”, “pp subito”, “cresc. molto”, “marc. il canto”. https://archive.org/details/elsombrerodetres00fall
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: London première cast, 1919
cues.text: At the London première on 22 July 1919 Léonide Massine, who also choreographed the ballet, danced the Miller, and Tamara Karsavina was the Miller’s Wife. Picasso designed the curtain, scenery and costumes.
cues.evidence: The first-performance cast and credits printed at the front of the J. & W. Chester piano score (1921): Massine as the Miller, Karsavina as the Miller’s Wife, choreography by Massine, curtain, scenery and costumes by Picasso, Alhambra Theatre, London, 22 July 1919. https://archive.org/details/elsombrerodetres00fall

cues.title: Final page, increasing tempo
cues.text: The last page of the piano score is marked “pochissimo più mosso, ma ritmico”, then “più animato” and “animando ancora sino il fine”. The tempo increases up to the final chords, which are marked fff. In the ballet a knock at the door follows, and the Law arrives with a warrant for the miller.
cues.evidence: J. & W. Chester piano score (1921), Danse du Meunier, printed page 41: “pochissimo più mosso, ma ritmico”, “più animato”, “animando ancora sino il fine”, “fff marcatiss.”. The printed synopsis, Part II (4)–(11), has the miller congratulated, a knock at the door, and the Alguacils arriving with a warrant. https://archive.org/details/elsombrerodetres00fall
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

fields.label: Work version
fields.value: Orchestral concert version of the Miller’s Dance, issued as the second of three dances from the ballet
fields.note: The 78 set carries Los vecinos, Danza del molinero and Danza final, the three dances of the second suite as the Los Angeles Philharmonic note lists them. The orchestral edition used and any cuts are unknown.

fields.label: Composition rights
fields.value: Falla died on 14 November 1946. Spanish law protects the works of authors who died before 7 December 1987 for life plus 80 years, so his music remains protected in Spain until the end of 2026; arrangements and modern editions carry their own rights
fields.note: A phonogram term assessment does not clear the composition, an arrangement or a modern score edition.

fields.label: Recording rights
fields.value: Territorial EU phonogram public-domain basis: published no later than 1954, before 1963
fields.note: The discs are listed in Columbia’s Spanish catalogue of 78 r.p.m. discs published up to 1 January 1954, and were recorded in 1928; the actual first issue date is not established here. This is a territorial phonogram basis, not US or worldwide clearance and not a Creative Commons licence.

composer.epithet: Composer from Cádiz who studied in Paris with Dukas and Debussy and is known for bringing Andalusian song and the guitar into orchestral music.
facts: Piano with José Tragó in Madrid (first prize, 1899); composition with Felipe Pedrell from 1901
Guided by Paul Dukas and Debussy; friends with Albéniz, Ravel and Ricardo Viñes
Gregorio Martínez Sierra and María Lejárraga · Diaghilev and Massine · Picasso · Lorca
An opera, a gitanería and a ballet, a nocturne for piano and orchestra, songs, a puppet opera and a harpsichord concerto; Atlántida unfinished

quote.text: For everything that concerns my trade, my homeland is Paris.
quote.source: Falla to Ignacio Zuloaga, Granada, 12 February 1923; Archivo Manuel de Falla

composer.background:
As a boy in Cádiz, Manuel de Falla ran an imaginary city called Colón. It had a council, newspapers and a theatre, and according to Roland-Manuel’s 1930 biography the great success of the day there was El conde de Villamediana, an opera seria composed and conducted by a certain Manuel de Falla. He kept the game going for six years. Falla was born on 23 November 1876 at 3 Plaza de Mina, and he first intended to be a writer. He told Roland-Manuel in 1928 that at seventeen a conviction at once timid and deep had turned him towards composition.

In Madrid he studied the piano with José Tragó and won the conservatoire’s first prize in 1899. Two years later he asked the Catalan musicologist Felipe Pedrell to teach him; from Pedrell, he told his biographer Jaime Pahissa, came the clearest and most solid guidance for his work.
